extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, practitioners, and stakeholders interested in U.S. Supreme Court decisions and DACA/administrative law litigation
extracted.subtask_short: APA judicial review of agency rescission
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes legal standards and procedural issues arising when courts review an agency's decision to rescind a policy (here, DHS's rescission of DACA), including APA arbitrary-and-capricious review, injunction/remedy scope, discovery of internal deliberations, and appointment/authority challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary and capricious standard (Administrative Procedure Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court held that DHS's decision to rescind DACA was "arbitrary and capricious" in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The majority emphasized that agency action must comply with the APA's procedural requirement to provide a reasoned explanation. An agency decision can be set aside as arbitrary and capricious if it fails to consider important aspects of the problem or provides an inadequate policy rationale. The Court remanded so DHS could reconsider, and made clear DHS could rescind the policy only if it supplied the justification required by the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned explanation / consideration of alternatives under APA
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must provide a reasoned explanation that addresses 'conspicuous issues' and alternatives when changing policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chief Justice Roberts wrote the agency "failed to consider the conspicuous issues of whether to retain forbearance and what if anything to do about the hardship to DACA recipients," demonstrating that agencies must (1) consider reasonable alternatives (e.g., forbearance), (2) weigh reliance and hardship effects on affected parties, and (3) show it appreciated the scope of its discretion. Failure to do so can render a rescission arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction standard — likelihood of success and irreparable harm
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court can order temporary relief when plaintiffs have demonstrated they are likely to suffer serious, irreparable harm and likely to succeed on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Alsup granted a preliminary injunction ordering DHS to maintain DACA while the lawsuit proceeded, stating that plaintiffs 'have clearly demonstrated that they are likely to suffer serious, irreparable harm.' This reflects the standard courts apply when deciding preliminary injunctive relief (likelihood of success on the merits; irreparable harm; balance of equities; public interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery / access to internal deliberative documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may order production of agencies' internal deliberative documents, but such orders can be contested and are subject to appellate and Supreme Court oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The district court ordered production of 'internal deliberative documents' behind the rescission decision. The government sought mandamus and a stay; the Ninth Circuit and Supreme Court were involved (Supreme Court temporarily halted the order and later set guidelines for access). This shows that access to internal agency deliberations is a litigable issue with limits (privileges, separation-of-powers concerns) and may require higher-court guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of relief/remedy in injunctions (existing vs new applicants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Injunctive relief can be limited in scope — e.g., to existing beneficiaries rather than expanding to accept new applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Alsup's ruling ordered DHS to renew deferred action for existing DACA recipients but did not require the government to accept new applications from those who had not previously received DACA. Subsequent district-court orders in other cases (after the Supreme Court decision) addressed acceptance of new applications; courts tailor injunctive remedies to the scope of demonstrated legal injury and the equities.

rubrics_metrics.name: DACA eligibility criteria (policy-side evaluative criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: The DACA program required applicants to have a clean criminal record to be eligible or continue renewal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes DACA recipients are required to have 'a clean criminal record' — specifically, no felony convictions, no significant misdemeanor convictions, or three or more misdemeanor convictions; these eligibility/criminal-history criteria are substantive policy standards used to evaluate applicants under DACA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of agency action taken by improperly appointed officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions taken by officials who were not properly appointed or lacked authority can be invalidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the Supreme Court decision, questions arose about the authority of acting DHS leaders (Kevin McAleenan, Chad Wolf). Judge Garaufis ruled McAleenan was never properly named Acting Secretary and thus lacked authority to pass it on, finding Wolf's July memo invalid — demonstrating that agency actions may be undone if the decision-maker lacked lawful authority under appointment/transfer rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and adequacy of policy rationale as a ground for challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of a detailed policy rationale and transparency in the decision-making process is a substantive vulnerability that invites legal challenge under the APA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics highlighted that the government 'failed to provide a detailed policy rationale,' which became a central issue in litigation. The article describes how lack of transparency in the agency's decision-making contributed to successful challenges and media/activist responses; courts scrutinize the sufficiency of the explanation an agency provides when changing established policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of judicial review — procedural (APA) vs. assessing legality of original program
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may confine review to whether an agency followed APA procedures in rescinding a program, rather than re-litigation of the original program's substantive legality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The majority limited its analysis to whether DHS complied with the APA's procedural requirements. Justice Thomas (dissent in part) argued the Court should have further evaluated the legality of the original DACA program. This highlights a contested criterion: whether review should focus on procedural adequacy of the rescission or also address the substantive legality of the underlying program.
